newsitem.title: USA: Atlanta Fed's Guynn sees '97 U.S. GDP up 2-2.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: Atlanta Fed's Guynn sees '97 U.S. GDP up 2-2.5 pct.

text.p: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta President Jack Guynn said he expects U.S. real gross domestic product to grow in a range of 2.0 percent to 2.5 percent in 1997, with the consumer price index rising near 3.0 percent.

Those forecasts, plus Guynn's forecast of a U.S. jobless rate near 5.5 percent, roughly mirror 1996 U.S. economic performance, noted Guynn in a speech to the German-American Chamber of Commerce in Atlanta.

"It looks like another year of moderate growth somewhere between two percent and 2-1/2 percent...unemployment continuing near the low level of 5-1/2 percent we've seen over the last two years and inflation, as measured by the CPI, continuing about its current three percent level," said Guynn.
Guynn noted that consumer spending "will be leading the way in the U.S. economy -- though not quite as vigorously as last year."
In addition, "business spending will be a source of strength in our economy again this year, albeit one that has been slowing down from its high point in 1994," Guynn added.
Despite the positive impact on growth from low unemployment, Guynn cited tight labor markets as a cause for concern.
"Job growth has continued to run well ahead of labor force growth," Guynn said. "Net-net, labor markets are at least a question mark in my mind as I look ahead into 1997 and beyond."
Meanwhile, consumer spending, while supported by job growth, consumer confidence and income growth, could fade under heavy consumer debt burdens, Guynn said.
"Growing levels of consumer indebtedness may begin to dampen expenditures," he said.
Guynn also discussed Canada and Mexico, the biggest and third-largest U.S. trading partners, where he said he expects solid economic growth in 1997.
"Both the Canadian and Mexican economies are expected to post moderate, yet healthy growth rates in 1997," said Guynn, forecasting 3-3/4 percent GDP growth in Mexico and three percent in Canada.
